solution:
The magnetic induction at the centre of a circular loop of radius \(r\) carrying current \(I\) is

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}\)

Rearranging for the current,

\(I = \dfrac{2rB}{\mu_0}\)

Here \(r = 12\ \text{cm} = 0.12\ \text{m}\), \(B = 6 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{T}\) and \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{Wb/Am}\).

\(I = \dfrac{2 \times 0.12 \times 6 \times 10^{-6}}{4 \times 3.142 \times 10^{-7}}\)

\(I = \dfrac{1.44 \times 10^{-6}}{1.2568 \times 10^{-6}}\)

\(I = 1.1458\ \text{A}\)

The magnetic moment of a single-turn loop is the product of the current and the area it encloses:

\(M = IA = I\pi r^{2}\)

\(M = 1.1458 \times 3.142 \times (0.12)^{2}\)

\(M = 1.1458 \times 3.142 \times 0.0144\)

\(M = 5.18 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{A m}^{2}\)

\(\therefore\) the magnetic moment of the loop is about \(5.18 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{A m}^{2}\).

[Textbook misprint: the question supplies "charge of electron \(= 1.62\times10^{-19}\) C". The accepted value is \(1.60\times10^{-19}\) C, and the book's own printed answer of \(6.643\times10^{-27}\) kg follows from 1.60 and not from 1.62; the latter would give \(6.72\times10^{-27}\) kg. The working above therefore uses \(1.60\times10^{-19}\) C, which also returns the accepted alpha-particle mass. The stem separately prints "a transverse a uniform magnetic field", with one article too many.]

Given: \(K = 10.00\) MeV, \(B = 1.851\) T, \(r = 24.60\) cm \(= 0.2460\) m, charge of the alpha particle \(q = +2e\).

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform field the magnetic force is centripetal, so
\(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\quad\Rightarrow\quad mv = qBr\)

The kinetic energy \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{(mv)^{2}}{2m}\), hence
\(m = \dfrac{(mv)^{2}}{2K} = \dfrac{(qBr)^{2}}{2K}\)

With \(e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\) C: \(q = 2e = 3.2\times10^{-19}\) C and \(K = 10.00\times10^{6}\times 1.6\times10^{-19} = 1.6\times10^{-12}\) J.
\(qBr = 3.2\times10^{-19}\times 1.851 \times 0.2460 = 1.457\times10^{-19}\) kg m/s
\(\therefore m = \dfrac{(1.457\times10^{-19})^{2}}{2\times 1.6\times10^{-12}} = \dfrac{2.123\times10^{-38}}{3.2\times10^{-12}}\)
\(\therefore m = 6.63\times10^{-27}\) kg

This is the accepted mass of the alpha particle (\(6.645\times10^{-27}\) kg, about 4 atomic mass units), which is the check that the working is sound.

Given: \(R = 12.3\) cm \(= 0.123\) m, \(B = 6.4\times10^{-6}\) T at the centre, single turn.

**Step 1: find the current.** At the centre of a circular loop,
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{2RB}{\mu_0} = \dfrac{2\times 0.123\times 6.4\times10^{-6}}{4\pi\times10^{-7}} = \dfrac{1.574\times10^{-6}}{1.2566\times10^{-6}}\)
\(\therefore I = 1.253\) A

**Step 2: magnetic moment.** For a plane current loop \(m = IA = I\pi R^{2}\):
\(m = 1.253 \times \pi \times (0.123)^{2} = 1.253 \times 0.04753\)
\(\therefore m = 5.955\times10^{-2}\) A m\(^2\)

The magnetic moment is directed along the axis of the loop, in the sense given by the right-hand rule applied to the circulating current.

Given: \(N = 300\) turns, diameter \(= 14\) cm so radius \(R = 7\) cm \(= 0.07\) m, \(I = 15\) A.

Area enclosed by one turn:

\(A = \pi R^{2} = \pi \times (0.07)^{2} = \pi \times 4.9 \times 10^{-3} = 1.5394 \times 10^{-2}\) m\(^{2}\)

The magnetic dipole moment of a coil of \(N\) turns is

\(m = NIA = 300 \times 15 \times 1.5394 \times 10^{-2} = 4500 \times 1.5394 \times 10^{-2}\)

\(\therefore m = 69.27\) A m\(^{2}\)

Check by a second route, using the diameter directly: \(m = NI\dfrac{\pi D^{2}}{4} = 300 \times 15 \times \dfrac{\pi \times (0.14)^{2}}{4} = 4500 \times 1.5394 \times 10^{-2} = 69.27\) A m\(^{2}\), the same value.

The magnetic dipole moment is directed along the axis of the coil, in the sense given by the right-hand rule.
note: 4500 x 1.539e-2 = 69.255, not the printed 69.27; the area to 5 figures, 1.5394e-2, gives 69.27.

From the figure at the end of this answer,
\(\tan\left(\dfrac{\delta}{2}\right) \cong \left(\dfrac{\delta}{2}\right)^{c} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{d}{4}\right)}{x_1}\)
and for a thin prism, \(\delta = A(\mu - 1)\)
\(\therefore d = 2\delta x_1 = 2A(\mu - 1)x_1\)
\(= 2\left(0.5 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180}\right)(1.5 - 1)10\)
\(= \dfrac{\pi}{36}\) cm
\(\lambda = 500\) nm \(= 5 \times 10^{-7}\) m,
\(L = 10\) cm \(+\ 90\) cm \(= 1\) m
Distance of \(20^{\text{th}}\) dark band from the central bright band, \(X_{20\text{D}} = \left(20 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)W\)
\(\therefore X_{20\text{D}} = (19.5)\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}\)
\(= \dfrac{19.5 \times \left(5 \times 10^{-7}\right) \times 1}{\left(\dfrac{\pi \times 10^{-2}}{36}\right)}\)
\(= \dfrac{19.5 \times 180 \times 10^{-5}}{\pi}\)
\(= 0.01117\) m \(= 1.117\) cm

Path difference at this location: for the \(n^{\text{th}}\) dark band it is \(\left(n - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda\), so

\(\Delta = 19.5 \times 5 \times 10^{-7} = 9.75 \times 10^{-6}\) m
note: 19.5 x 180e-5 / pi = 0.01117 m (printed 0.1117 m); the asked path difference, 19.5 lambda = 9.75e-6 m, was never given.

solution:
Given: fundamental frequency \( n = 300 \) Hz, speed of sound \( v = 340\ \mathrm{m\ s}^{-1} \), tube OPEN at both ends.

For a pipe open at both ends an antinode forms at each end, so in the fundamental mode the air column holds half a wavelength:
\( L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \qquad \therefore \lambda = 2L \)

\( \therefore n = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{v}{2L} \)

\( \therefore L = \dfrac{v}{2n} = \dfrac{340}{2 \times 300} = \dfrac{340}{600} \)

\( \therefore L = 0.5667\ \mathrm{m} \)

\( \therefore \) the length of the tube in the fundamental mode is about \( 0.5667 \) m \( \approx 56.7 \) cm.

(The end correction has been neglected here; including it, this \( L \) would be the corrected length \( l + 2e \), so the actual pipe would be slightly shorter.)
